To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“The risk of reactivation of LTBI was associated with a high preinfection serum level of C-reactive protein, an inflammatory biomarker, and that this association was independent of the level of preinfection serum IgG antibody to Mycobacterium tuberculosis.”
the presence of a biomarker at the time of hospitalization for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is a strong predictor of subsequent mortality.
“The presence of a high baseline CRP level in the absence of an inflammatory condition is a risk factor for hospitalization due to a pneumonia.”
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the immune system and inflammation as a risk factor for the progression of latent tuberculosis (TB) infection to active disease (reactivation).
the role of the innate immune system in host defense and disease.
the development and validation of biomarker panels to identify patients at high risk of developing reactivation of latent TB infection and of hospitalization due to pneumonia.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk for reactivation of latent TB in patients who are treated for pneumonia is low, but it is difficult to quantify.
there is a need for further investigation into the association between the biomarkers of inflammation and the risk of reactivation of latent TB infection.
the risk of death is increased in patients with severe pneumonia and that this risk is higher in patients with severe CAP.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we found that patients who had an episode of pneumonia had an increased risk of subsequent hospitalizations for a number of reasons.
the risk of death in the 30 days after a pneumonia hospitalization is increased in the presence of a high inflammatory response.
a biomarker profile that can predict the risk of hospitalization for pneumonia in the elderly is possible.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use biomarkers to predict which people will develop pneumonia.
the inflammatory response to pneumonia may be an early marker of risk of subsequent hospitalizations and mortality.
the risk for death from pneumonia in the 2 weeks after discharge is not related to the inflammatory and coagulant response at the time of discharge.
